qs.q: How does lysogenic conversion affect a host bacterium such as Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
o: It grants the bacterium traits like diphtheria toxin production
It converts the bacterial chromosome into a segmented RNA
It destroys the host cell via rapid lytic replication
It permanently prevents any future bacteriophage infections
qs.e: Lysogenic conversion occurs when a prophage imparts new genetic traits to the host bacterium, such as the tox gene required for Corynebacterium diphtheriae to produce diphtheria toxin. The lytic cycle, rather than lysogenic conversion, destroys the host cell immediately.

qs.q: The presence of a pseudomembrane in the throat, a thick, grayish-white layer, is a hallmark of diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
qs.e: A pseudomembrane is a characteristic feature of diphtheria. It is formed by necrotic tissue, fibrin, and bacteria on the surface of the pharynx and tonsils. While severe strep throat can sometimes have exudates, a true pseudomembrane is indicative of diphtheria.

qs.q: The Elek test is used to detect toxigenicity of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It involves placing a filter paper strip soaked in antitoxin onto an agar plate inoculated with the bacterium. If the bacterium produces diphtheria toxin, a visible precipitation line will form where the toxin meets the antitoxin.
qs.e: The Elek test is a qualitative in vitro assay used to determine if a strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae is toxigenic (i.e., capable of producing diphtheria toxin). It is a serological test based on the precipitation reaction between the produced toxin and specific antitoxin.
